etymology: From Latin omnis, all, and potens, powerful. The Authorized Version uses it once, in the great multitude's shout in Revelation 19; the same divine title is rendered Almighty everywhere else.
biblical_def: And I heard as it were the voice of a great multitude, and as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of mighty thunderings, saying, Alleluia: for the Lord God omnipotent reigneth. John piles three sounds on top of each other to describe one shout, and the shout is a single sentence of theology. The context is the fall of Babylon and the announcement that follows: Let us be glad and rejoice, and give honour to him: for the marriage of the Lamb is come, and his wife hath made herself ready. Omnipotence in Scripture is never an abstract attribute considered on its own. It is always attached to something God is doing — making heaven and earth by his great power and stretched out arm, so that there is nothing too hard for him; appearing to a man of ninety and nine as the Almighty God with a covenant promise; and here, reigning, at the end, with the marriage supper prepared. The dictionary holds omnipotence in the classical sense: God can do all his holy will, and cannot do what is contrary to his nature, since he cannot lie, cannot deny himself, and cannot be tempted with evil. That is not a limitation on his power but the definition of it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): almighty; possessing unlimited power; all-powerful; an attribute of God only.
webster_full: OMNIPOTENT, a. Almighty; possessing unlimited power; all powerful.
OMNIPOTENT, n. The Almighty; God, who is all powerful; an appellation of the Supreme Being.
ALMIGHTY, a. Possessing all power; omnipotent; being of unlimited might; being of boundless sufficiency.
ALLELUIA, n. Praise to Jehovah; a word used to denote pious joy and exultation, chiefly in hymns and anthems.
ATTRIBUTE, n. That which is inherent in a subject; an inherent or essential quality or property.
scriptures: Rev 19:6
And I heard as it were the voice of a great multitude, and as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of mighty thunderings, saying, Alleluia: for the Lord God omnipotent reigneth.
Rev 19:7
Let us be glad and rejoice, and give honour to him: for the marriage of the Lamb is come, and his wife hath made herself ready.
Gen 17:1
And when Abram was ninety years old and nine, the LORD appeared to Abram, and said unto him, I am the Almighty God; walk before me, and be thou perfect.
Ah Lord GOD! behold, thou hast made the heaven and the earth by thy great power and stretched out arm, and there is nothing too hard for thee:
corruption_summary: Divine power is diminished by open theism and process theology into a persuasive influence within history, or turned into a bare abstraction in which anything at all is possible to God; Scripture ties it to his will, his word, and his throne.
corruption_paragraphs: Open theism, following Pinnock, Boyd, and Sanders, denies exhaustive divine foreknowledge and makes God a responder to a future he does not yet know; process theology goes further and denies divine immutability and omnipotence outright, leaving a deity who lures rather than governs. Both are named errors and the dictionary names them. Revelation 19 does not describe a God who hopes the outcome goes well. The Lord God omnipotent reigneth — present, settled, and shouted like thunder by a multitude no man could number, in the hearing of a church that had been under the sword.

The opposite error treats omnipotence as bare arbitrary capacity, as though God could lie, or cease to be God, or make himself unholy. Scripture forbids it: God, that cannot lie; he cannot deny himself; God cannot be tempted with evil. His power is the power of his own nature, and therefore it is never a threat to his goodness. That is precisely why the doctrine is a comfort rather than a terror to his people, and why the same voice that thunders his omnipotence in verse 6 announces the marriage of the Lamb in verse 7.
roots_summary: Greek pantokrator (G3841), the ruler of all, the Almighty; basileuo (G936), to reign; Hebrew Shadday (H7706), the Almighty.
roots_lines: Greek pantokrator (G3841) — all-ruling, almighty; rendered omnipotent at Revelation 19:6.
Greek basileuo (G936) — to reign, to be king; the Lord God omnipotent reigneth.
Hebrew Shadday (H7706) — the Almighty; I am the Almighty God.
Hebrew pala' (H6381) — to be wonderful, to be too hard; there is nothing too hard for thee.
Greek allelouia (G239) — praise ye the LORD; the shout of the multitude.

“I am the Almighty God” — the same title to Abram.
“there is nothing too hard for thee” — Jeremiah, with a field bought under siege.

pos: adj. (not liable to death; the King eternal)
etymology: From Latin immortalis, from in-, not, and mors, death; the Greek is literally incorruptible. The Authorized Version uses it once, in Paul's doxology to the King eternal, immortal, invisible.
biblical_def: Now unto the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only wise God, be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen. The doxology bursts out of the middle of Paul's account of his own conversion, immediately after he has called himself the chief of sinners and said he obtained mercy as a pattern for others. Four things are said of God in four words — eternal, immortal, invisible, only wise — and the first Timothy epistle says the second of them more exactly a few chapters later: who only hath immortality, dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto. God alone has deathlessness in himself; every creature that lives for ever does so as a gift. That is why the New Testament speaks of immortality as something brought to light and put on rather than possessed by nature: our Saviour Jesus Christ hath abolished death, and hath brought life and immortality to light through the gospel; and this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality. The Christian hope is not that the soul was always going to survive, but that the body will be raised.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): having no principle of alteration or corruption; exempt from liability to death; imperishable; in Scripture, an attribute of God, who only hath immortality.
webster_full: IMMORTAL, a. Having no principle of alteration or corruption; exempt from liability to death; imperishable.
IMMORTALITY, n. Exemption from death and annihilation; life destined to endure without end.
INCORRUPTION, n. Incapacity of corruption; exemption from decay.
ETERNAL, a. Without beginning or end of existence; everlasting; an attribute of God.
DOXOLOGY, n. In Christian worship, a hymn in praise of the Almighty.
scriptures: Now unto the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only wise God, be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.
Who only hath immortality, dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto; whom no man hath seen, nor can see: to whom be honour and power everlasting. Amen.
But is now made manifest by the appearing of our Saviour Jesus Christ, who hath abolished death, and hath brought life and immortality to light through the gospel:
For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality.
corruption_summary: Christian hope is reduced to the survival of an immortal soul, a Greek idea rather than a biblical one; Scripture reserves immortality to God by nature and promises his people a raised body.
corruption_paragraphs: Popular Christian language about the afterlife is largely Platonic: the body is a shell, the soul escapes, and heaven is a destination for disembodied spirits. The New Testament's hope is elsewhere. Paul does speak of being absent from the body and present with the Lord, and that intermediate state is real and blessed, but he calls it being unclothed and says he would rather be clothed upon, that mortality might be swallowed up of life. The resurrection of the body is the actual promise, and 1 Corinthians 15 argues that if there is no resurrection then the faith is vain and the dead in Christ are perished. A hope that stops at the immortality of the soul has stopped one whole doctrine short.

The other correction is that God only hath immortality. The soul's endless existence, whether in blessedness or in punishment, is a gift and a sentence rather than a property it owns. The dictionary therefore holds eternal conscious punishment for the unredeemed against annihilationism, and holds the bodily resurrection of the just and the unjust, because both stand or fall on the same texts. And the one who abolished death brought life and immortality to light through the gospel — not by discovering a fact about human nature, but by rising.
roots_lines: Greek aphthartos (G862) — incorruptible, not liable to decay; rendered immortal at 1 Timothy 1:17.
Greek athanasia (G110) — deathlessness, immortality; who only hath immortality.
Greek aoratos (G517) — unseen, invisible; the King eternal, immortal, invisible.
Greek katargeo (G2673) — to render inoperative, to abolish; hath abolished death.
Greek enduo (G1746) — to put on, to clothe; this mortal must put on immortality.
usage: “the King eternal, immortal, invisible” — the single occurrence.
“Who only hath immortality” — immortality reserved to God by nature.
“this mortal must put on immortality” — the creature's hope, and it is bodily.

etymology: From Latin in-, not, and poenitens, repenting. The Authorized Version uses it once, of the hardness and impenitent heart that treasures up wrath.
biblical_def: But after thy hardness and impenitent heart treasurest up unto thyself wrath against the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God. The metaphor is what makes the verse unforgettable. A man who will not repent is accumulating, laying up a store, and what he is storing is wrath — against a day, and that day is named as the revelation of the righteous judgment of God. The verse before it explains what he is despising while he does it: or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance? Every day of unpunished sin is a mercy misread as indifference. And the verse after states the standard of that day without qualification: who will render to every man according to his deeds. Revelation shows the same hardness at the end of history, under plagues that leave no room for doubt about their source: men were scorched with great heat, and blasphemed the name of God, which hath power over these plagues: and they repented not to give him glory. Suffering by itself softens nobody. Only the goodness of God, applied by his Spirit, leads to repentance.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): not repenting of sin; not contrite; of a hard heart; obdurate; not sensible of one's guilt.
webster_full: IMPENITENT, a. Not penitent; not repenting of sin; not contrite; of a hard heart; obdurate.
IMPENITENCE, n. Want of penitence or repentance; hardness of heart; obduracy.
REPENTANCE, n. Real penitence; sorrow or deep contrition for sin, as an offense and dishonor to God.
FORBEARANCE, n. The exercise of patience; long suffering; indulgence towards those who injure us.
LONGSUFFERING, n. Bearing injuries or provocation for a long time; patience of offense.
scriptures: Rom 2:5
But after thy hardness and impenitent heart treasurest up unto thyself wrath against the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God;
Rom 2:4
Or despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering; not knowing that the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance?
Rom 2:6
Who will render to every man according to his deeds:
Rev 16:9
And men were scorched with great heat, and blasphemed the name of God, which hath power over these plagues: and they repented not to give him glory.
corruption_summary: Delay in judgment is read as evidence that judgment is not coming, or that God is indifferent to sin; Romans says the delay is the riches of his goodness and forbearance, given to lead men to repentance.
corruption_paragraphs: Peter answers the same objection in its plainest form. There shall come in the last days scoffers, saying, Where is the promise of his coming? for since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation. The answer is not that judgment has been cancelled but that its delay has a purpose: the Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance. Time is the space God gives for turning, and Romans 2 says that a man can spend that space accumulating the opposite.

The word treasurest is the most searching thing in the verse, because it makes impenitence an activity rather than a state. Nobody drifts into a treasury; it is filled deposit by deposit, and the depositor is always the man himself. And Revelation shows that the accumulation does not reverse under pressure. They gnawed their tongues for pain, and blasphemed the God of heaven because of their pains and their sores, and repented not of their deeds. The only thing that ever produced repentance in a sinner is the goodness of God, and that is where Romans 2 says to look.
roots_summary: Greek ametanoetos (G279), unrepentant; sklerotes (G4643), hardness; thesaurizo (G2343), to lay up in store.
roots_lines: Greek ametanoetos (G279) — unrepentant, impenitent; the one occurrence, Romans 2:5.

Greek chrestotes (G5544) — goodness, kindness; the riches of his goodness.

“the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance” — what the delay is for.
“they repented not to give him glory” — hardness under the plagues.

pos: n. (subjection to death; the condition of this present body)
etymology: From Latin mortalitas, from mors, death. The Authorized Version uses it once, in Paul's account of the groaning of this life and the clothing that ends it.
biblical_def: For we that are in this tabernacle do groan, being burdened: not for that we would be unclothed, but clothed upon, that mortality might be swallowed up of life. Paul's figure runs through the whole chapter. The body is a tabernacle, a tent, and the groaning in it is real: he does not pretend that dying is easy or that the wearing out of a body is a small thing. But the longing he describes is not a longing to be rid of the body. It is a longing to be further clothed — for we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. Between the tent and the building lies the intermediate state, which Paul names with equal confidence: we are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord. That is blessed and it is not the end. The end is the resurrection, when mortality is not escaped but swallowed: so when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): subjection to death, or the necessity of dying; also, death, or the frequency of death; in Scripture, the condition of this tabernacle, to be swallowed up of life.
webster_full: MORTALITY, n. Subjection to death, or the necessity of dying.
MORTALITY, n. Death; as the mortality of a season.
TABERNACLE, n. A tent; a temporary habitation; in Scripture, the present body as the soul's tent.
DISSOLVE, v.t. To loose; to separate the parts of; to break up; as, the earthly house of this tabernacle dissolved.
VICTORY, n. Conquest; the defeat of an enemy in battle, or of an antagonist in contest.
scriptures: For we that are in this tabernacle do groan, being burdened: not for that we would be unclothed, but clothed upon, that mortality might be swallowed up of life.
For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.
We are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord.
So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory.
corruption_summary: Death is managed as a natural stage of life to be accepted, or denied altogether by a culture that hides it; Scripture calls it an enemy, has the apostle groaning under it, and promises that it will be swallowed up rather than befriended.
corruption_paragraphs: Two modern strategies for death both fail the Christian. The first hides it, keeping the dying out of sight and speaking of passing rather than dying. The second domesticates it, calling it a natural part of life and asking the bereaved to make peace with it. Scripture will do neither. Death entered by sin, it is called the last enemy that shall be destroyed, and the Lord himself groaned in the spirit and wept at a grave he was about to open. Paul groans, being burdened, and records it in an inspired letter. Grief is not a failure of faith.

What Christian hope adds is not calm but a direction. We sorrow, but not as others which have no hope. The tent is wearing out and there is a building; the body will be sown in corruption and raised in incorruption; and mortality is not accepted but swallowed up of life. That last verb is the whole difference. Death is not reasoned with, made peaceful, or accommodated. It is consumed, and the taunt that follows is the church's at every graveside: O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?
roots_summary: Greek thnetos (G2349), mortal, liable to death; skenos (G4636), a tent or tabernacle; katapino (G2666), to swallow up.
roots_lines: Greek thnetos (G2349) — liable to death, mortal; rendered mortality at 2 Corinthians 5:4.

“we that are in this tabernacle do groan, being burdened” — grief permitted.

pos: n. (training, discipline, upbringing; the father's charge in Ephesians 6)
etymology: From Old French norriture, nourishment, from Latin nutrire, to feed; and so a rearing that both feeds and forms. The Greek word Paul uses is paideia, the whole discipline of a child. It occurs once.
biblical_def: And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord. The verse is addressed to fathers specifically, and it has a negative and a positive half that belong together. Provoke not to wrath — the parallel in Colossians gives the reason, lest they be discouraged. Then the charge: bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord, which is discipline and verbal instruction together, and of the Lord, meaning his and not the father's own. The Old Testament had described the method in detail long before: and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up. That is not a curriculum but a life lived audibly in front of children. Proverbs gives the promise the whole enterprise leans on: Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it. And the paragraph opens with the child's own duty, which the father cannot discharge for him: Children, obey your parents in the Lord: for this is right.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): that which nourishes; food; diet; also education; instruction; the discipline which forms manners and character.
webster_full: NURTURE, n. That which nourishes; food; diet.
NURTURE, n. Education; instruction; the discipline which forms the manners and character.
ADMONITION, n. Gentle reproof; counseling against a fault; instruction in duties; caution; direction.
PROVOKE, v.t. To call into action; to arouse; to excite; to make angry; to offend.
DISCIPLINE, n. Education; instruction; cultivation and improvement, comprehending instruction in arts, science, correction, and government.
scriptures: Eph 6:4
And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.
Eph 6:1
Children, obey your parents in the Lord: for this is right.
Deu 6:7
And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
Pro 22:6
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
corruption_summary: Parenting is outsourced to school, church programme, or screen, or else reduced to management of behaviour; Scripture charges fathers personally with a formation that is both discipline and instruction, and makes it the Lord's and not the parent's own.
corruption_paragraphs: Two failures sit on either side of Ephesians 6:4. The first is harshness, which the verse names directly — provoke not your children to wrath — and Colossians explains, lest they be discouraged. A father can be doctrinally correct and crush a child, and Scripture treats that as disobedience to this command rather than as rigour. The second failure is abdication, handing the formation to institutions and calling it education. Deuteronomy 6 assumes a father talking about the commandments in the house, on the road, at bedtime, and at waking, which no programme can do on his behalf.

The dictionary holds the creational order this verse assumes: the father bears the charge, the mother is honoured with him in the fifth commandment, and children are commanded to obey their parents in the Lord. And the phrase of the Lord keeps the whole thing from becoming a family religion, because the nurture and admonition belong to Christ and not to the man administering them. Proverbs 22:6 is a proverb and not a contract — it states the ordinary way God works and is not a guarantee that binds him — but it is the promise on which generations of faithful fathers have laboured, and it remains true of the way God ordinarily deals with households.
roots_summary: Greek paideia (G3809), the training and discipline of a child; nouthesia (G3559), admonition, warning instruction; ektrepho (G1625), to rear up to maturity.

Hebrew shanan (H8150) — to whet, to sharpen, to teach diligently; thou shalt teach them diligently.

“provoke not your children to wrath” — the negative half of the charge.
“thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children” — the method, in Deuteronomy.

pos: v. (knew beforehand; in Paul, set his love upon beforehand)
etymology: From fore, before, and knew, rendering Greek proginosko. In Scripture to know is very often to acknowledge, to choose, to set one's love upon, and not merely to be informed about.
biblical_def: God hath not cast away his people which he foreknew. Paul is answering whether God has abandoned Israel, and his answer rests on a word about God's prior act. The parallel in Romans 8 gives the chain in full: for whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren. Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified. Every link has the same set of people in it, and every verb is God's. The object of foreknew is not a fact about persons but the persons themselves — whom he did foreknow — which is why the Reformed tradition reads it as God's prior setting of his love, in the same sense as Amos, You only have I known of all the families of the earth, and Jeremiah, Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee. Paul's conclusion in Romans 11 is the doctrine stated plainly: even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): knew beforehand; had previous knowledge of; in Scripture, God's prior knowing of his people, which Paul joins to predestination, calling, justification, and glory.
webster_full: FOREKNOW, v.t. To have previous knowledge of; to foresee.
FOREKNOWLEDGE, n. Knowledge of a thing before it happens; prescience.
PREDESTINATE, v.t. To predetermine or foreordain; to appoint or ordain beforehand by an unchangeable purpose.
ELECTION, n. In theology, the choice of persons to eternal life; divine choice; predetermination of God.
REMNANT, n. Residue; that which is left after the separation, removal or destruction of a part.
scriptures: Rom 11:2
God hath not cast away his people which he foreknew. Wot ye not what the scripture saith of Elias? how he maketh intercession to God against Israel, saying,
Rom 8:29
For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren.
Rom 8:30
Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified.
Rom 11:5
Even so then at this present time also there is a remnant according to the election of grace.
corruption_summary: Foreknowledge is redefined as God's advance sight of who would believe, making election a response to foreseen faith; the text says whom he foreknew, not what, and the whole chain of verbs belongs to God.
corruption_paragraphs: The foreseen-faith reading is the standard alternative and it founders on the grammar and on the rest of the paragraph. Paul writes whom he did foreknow, with persons as the object, and the chain that follows leaves no room for a human contribution at any link: predestinated, called, justified, glorified, all with the same subject and the same set. If the ground of election were foreseen faith, then election would be conditioned on the creature, and Romans 9 forecloses it: it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy. Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated — said before the children were born, neither having done any good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand.

The biblical sense of knowing settles the matter. Adam knew Eve; the Lord says of Israel, You only have I known of all the families of the earth, therefore I will punish you; and Christ will say to the lawless, I never knew you — which cannot mean he lacked information. To be foreknown is to have been loved beforehand. That is why Paul can build the strongest assurance in Scripture on it, ending, who shall separate us from the love of Christ? and answering that neither death, nor life, nor things present, nor things to come shall be able to separate us.

pos: n. pl. (kidnappers; those who seize and sell human beings)
etymology: From men and stealer, rendering Greek andrapodistes, a slave-dealer, one who enslaves a free man. The Authorized Version uses it once, in Paul's list of those the law is made for.
biblical_def: For whoremongers, for them that defile themselves with mankind, for menstealers, for liars, for perjured persons, and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine. Paul is explaining the proper use of the law, which is not made for a righteous man, but for the lawless and disobedient, and his catalogue runs in the order of the Decalogue — murderers of fathers and mothers against the fifth commandment, manslayers against the sixth, whoremongers and the defilers against the seventh, menstealers against the eighth, liars and perjured persons against the ninth. Manstealing is the eighth commandment's worst form: not the theft of a man's goods but the theft of the man. The Mosaic law made it capital without qualification, and without regard to what became of him afterwards: he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death. And Paul closes the list by measuring all of it against the gospel: according to the glorious gospel of the blessed God, which was committed to my trust.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one that steals and carries away a man or men; a kidnapper; in Scripture, named among those contrary to sound doctrine.
webster_full: MAN-STEALER, n. One that steals and carries away a man or men; a kidnapper.
KIDNAP, v.t. To steal and carry away any person whatever, whether man, woman or child.
LAWLESS, a. Not subject to law; unrestrained by law; contrary to law; illegal.
SOUND, a. Firm; strong; valid; solid; well-founded; as sound doctrine.
DECALOGUE, n. The ten commandments or precepts given by God to Moses at mount Sinai.
scriptures: For whoremongers, for them that defile themselves with mankind, for menstealers, for liars, for perjured persons, and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine;

Knowing this, that the law is not made for a righteous man, but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and for sinners, for unholy and profane, for murderers of fathers and murderers of mothers, for manslayers,
And he that stealeth a man, and selleth him, or if he be found in his hand, he shall surely be put to death.
According to the glorious gospel of the blessed God, which was committed to my trust.
corruption_summary: The Bible is said to sanction slavery, and the texts that condemn its foundation are passed over; Exodus makes manstealing a capital crime and Paul lists menstealers among those whose trade is contrary to sound doctrine.
corruption_paragraphs: The chattel slavery of the Atlantic trade rested entirely on manstealing: men and women seized, sold, and held as property who had never been captives of war, debtors, or convicts. Scripture pronounces the death penalty on the first link of that chain and names the traders among the lawless. This was not a nineteenth-century discovery. The abolitionists argued it from these texts, and the defenders of the trade had to work around them, which is the usual position of those defending an institution the Bible condemns at its root.

The regulation of servitude within Israel — release in the seventh year, freedom for a maimed servant, refuge for a runaway rather than his return, sabbath rest extended to servants, and the jubilee — belongs to a different institution and a different world from the one these texts condemn. And the New Testament's trajectory runs one way: Paul sends Onesimus back as a brother beloved, tells servants who may be made free to use it rather, commands masters to remember they have a Master in heaven, and places menstealers in a list with murderers. The dictionary names the trade by the name Scripture gives it.
roots_summary: Greek andrapodistes (G405), a slave-dealer, a manstealer; anomos (G459), lawless; Hebrew ganab (H1589), to steal.
roots_lines: Greek andrapodistes (G405) — an enslaver, a manstealer; the one occurrence, 1 Timothy 1:10.
Greek anomos (G459) — lawless, without law; the law is made for the lawless.
Greek hugiaino (G5198) — to be sound or healthy; contrary to sound doctrine.
Hebrew ganab (H1589) — to steal; he that stealeth a man.
Hebrew muwth (H4191) — to die, to be put to death; he shall surely be put to death.
usage: “for menstealers, for liars, for perjured persons” — the single occurrence.
“he that stealeth a man, and selleth him” — a capital crime under the law.
“contrary to sound doctrine” — the category Paul assigns it to.

pos: n. (a factious man; one who divides the church by choosing his own opinion)
etymology: From Greek hairetikos, from haireomai, to choose — a man who takes his own party. The Authorized Version spells it with the -ck and uses it once, in Paul's instruction to Titus.
biblical_def: A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject. The instruction is a procedure, not an outburst, and the two admonitions are the heart of it. The man is warned, warned again, and only then rejected, and Paul explains why the rejection is warranted at that point: knowing that he that is such is subverted, and sinneth, being condemned of himself. The self-condemnation is the diagnostic. After two plain warnings, a man who persists is no longer mistaken but choosing. The context is a chapter about avoiding what is unprofitable: but avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain. The Greek word behind heretick is about faction and self-chosen party as much as about doctrinal error; the two usually travel together, which is why Paul also says heresies are among the works of the flesh, beside variance, emulations, wrath, and strife. And Corinthians states the strange providence in it: for there must be also heresies among you, that they which are approved may be made manifest among you.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): one who holds to a heresy; one who maintains an opinion repugnant to the established faith; in Scripture, a factious man to be rejected after two admonitions.
webster_full: HERETIC, n. A person under any religion, but particularly the christian, who holds and teaches opinions repugnant to the established faith.
HERESY, n. A fundamental error in religion, or an error of opinion respecting some fundamental doctrine of religion.
SCHISM, n. In church affairs, a division or separation; a breach of unity among people of the same religious faith.
ADMONITION, n. Gentle reproof; counseling against a fault; instruction in duties; caution; direction.
EXCOMMUNICATION, n. The act of ejecting from a church, or cutting off from the communion of the faithful.
scriptures: Tit 3:10
A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject;
Tit 3:11
Knowing that he that is such is subverted, and sinneth, being condemned of himself.
Tit 3:9
But avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain.
For there must be also heresies among you, that they which are approved may be made manifest among you.
corruption_summary: The word is used either as a weapon against anyone who disagrees about anything, or retired entirely on the ground that no one may be excluded; Paul's instruction has two warnings before it, a specific diagnosis, and a defined end.
corruption_paragraphs: Two abuses of Titus 3:10 are equally common. The first skips the admonitions, applying the label to a first disagreement and treating every difference as a fundamental one. Scripture's own practice is more patient: Paul withstood Peter to the face over a real error and did not reject him; Apollos was taken aside and taught the way of God more perfectly; the weak brother in Romans 14 is to be received, not disputed with. The word is reserved for the man who has been warned twice and persists in dividing.

The second abuse retires the category altogether, on the view that exclusion is always unloving. That reading has to discard a great deal: mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned; and avoid them. A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump. If there come any unto you, and bring not this doctrine, receive him not into your house. Church discipline is commanded, its purpose is restorative — that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus — and a church that cannot say no eventually cannot say anything.
roots_summary: Greek hairetikos (G141), factious, heretical; hairesis (G139), a choosing, a party, a sect; ekstrepho (G1612), to turn inside out, to subvert.
roots_lines: Greek hairetikos (G141) — factious, given to party spirit; the one occurrence, Titus 3:10.
Greek hairesis (G139) — a choosing, a sect, a party; there must be also heresies among you.
Greek nouthesia (G3559) — admonition, warning; after the first and second admonition.
Greek ekstrepho (G1612) — to turn out, to pervert, to subvert; he that is such is subverted.
Greek autokatakritos (G843) — self-condemned; being condemned of himself.
usage: “after the first and second admonition reject” — the single occurrence.
“being condemned of himself” — the diagnosis that warrants it.
“avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions” — the surrounding counsel.

pos: n. (a formal public speech; the last one Herod ever gave)
etymology: From Latin oratio, a speech, from orare, to speak or plead. The Authorized Version uses it once, of the address Herod made from his throne in royal apparel, after which he was smitten.
biblical_def: And upon a set day Herod, arrayed in royal apparel, sat upon his throne, and made an oration unto them. The people gave a shout, saying, It is the voice of a god, and not of a man. And immediately the angel of the Lord smote him, because he gave not God the glory: and he was eaten of worms, and gave up the ghost. Luke gives the whole sequence in three verses and the reason for the judgment in six words: because he gave not God the glory. The sin was not making the speech, nor the royal apparel, nor even the crowd's flattery, which Herod did not arrange. It was receiving what belonged to God and saying nothing. Compare Paul and Barnabas at Lystra, who rent their clothes and ran in among the people to stop precisely this, and Peter lifting Cornelius off the floor. Herod sat still. And then Luke sets the verse that always follows such a scene in Acts, with a deliberate contrast: But the word of God grew and multiplied. A king dies eaten of worms in one sentence, and the next sentence is about the thing that actually grows.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a speech or discourse composed according to the rules of oratory, and spoken in public; in Scripture, the address after which Herod was smitten for not giving God the glory.
webster_full: ORATION, n. A speech or discourse composed according to the rules of oratory, and spoken in public.
ORATOR, n. A public speaker; in modern usage, a person of eloquence.
FLATTERY, n. False praise; commendation bestowed for the purpose of gaining favor and influence.
GLORY, n. Praise ascribed in adoration; honor; in Scripture, the exhibition of the divine perfections.
PRESUMPTION, n. Arrogance; blind or headstrong confidence; unreasonable adventurousness.
scriptures: And upon a set day Herod, arrayed in royal apparel, sat upon his throne, and made an oration unto them.
And the people gave a shout, saying, It is the voice of a god, and not of a man.
And immediately the angel of the Lord smote him, because he gave not God the glory: and he was eaten of worms, and gave up the ghost.
But the word of God grew and multiplied.
corruption_summary: Receiving honour that belongs to God is treated as a failure of modesty rather than as theft; Luke records a death sentence executed on the spot, with the reason stated as giving not God the glory.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 12 is arranged as a contrast and the arrangement is the argument. The chapter opens with Herod killing James with the sword and arresting Peter to please the people; it has the church praying and an angel opening an iron gate of its own accord; and it ends with the same king on a throne, receiving divine honours and struck down. Two men in prison, two very different outcomes, and one conclusion: But the word of God grew and multiplied. The kings of the earth set themselves against the Lord and against his anointed, and the book of Acts keeps noting quietly what happens to them and what happens to the word.

The sin named is precise and it is worth naming precisely, because the modern version is usually gentler than a throne and royal apparel. A man receives credit he knows is not his and does not correct it. A ministry accepts a reputation it has not earned. A leader lets an impression stand because contradicting it would cost something. Herod did nothing but stay seated. And the doctrine underneath is the simplest in Scripture: my glory will I not give to another.
roots_summary: Greek demegoreo (G1215), to address a public assembly, to make an oration; skolekobrotos (G4662), eaten of worms; doxa (G1391), glory.

Greek skolekobrotos (G4662) — worm-eaten; he was eaten of worms.
Greek doxa (G1391) — glory, honour, praise; because he gave not God the glory.
Greek epiphoneo (G2019) — to shout out, to cry aloud; the people gave a shout.

“because he gave not God the glory” — the stated reason for the judgment.
“But the word of God grew and multiplied” — the sentence that follows.

pos: interj. (Aramaic, arise; in Talitha cumi, the word spoken to Jairus' daughter)
etymology: Aramaic qumi, the feminine imperative of qum, to arise. Mark preserves the actual syllables the Lord spoke and then translates them, which he does only a handful of times in his Gospel.
biblical_def: And he took the damsel by the hand, and said unto her, Talitha cumi; which is, being interpreted, Damsel, I say unto thee, arise. Mark has kept the sound of the words, which means somebody in that room remembered them exactly — and only Peter, James, John, and the parents were in it. The occasion is the hardest in the Gospel: Jairus, a ruler of the synagogue, had begged for his little daughter, the journey was interrupted by the woman with the issue of blood, and while Christ was still speaking the message came that the child was dead and there was no need to trouble the Master further. His answer to the father, spoken over that news, is the sentence the dictionary would give every believer at a deathbed: Be not afraid, only believe. Then the room is cleared of the mourners, the hand is taken, and two words in the family's own language raise a twelve-year-old girl. And straightway the damsel arose, and walked; and they were astonished with a great astonishment. He commanded that something should be given her to eat, which is the detail that proves it was a girl and not a vision.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for this Aramaic word; Mark interprets it himself — Talitha cumi, being interpreted, Damsel, I say unto thee, arise.
webster_full: ARISE, v.i. To ascend, mount up or move upward; to get out of bed; to rise from the dead.
DAMSEL, n. A young woman; a girl; a maiden.
INTERPRET, v.t. To explain the meaning of words in a different language to one who does not understand them.
ASTONISH, v.t. To stun; to strike dumb with sudden fear, terror, surprise or wonder.
RESURRECTION, n. A rising again; the revival of the dead of the human race, or their return from the grave.
scriptures: Mar 5:41
And he took the damsel by the hand, and said unto her, Talitha cumi; which is, being interpreted, Damsel, I say unto thee, arise.
Mar 5:42
And straightway the damsel arose, and walked; for she was of the age of twelve years. And they were astonished with a great astonishment.
Mar 5:36
As soon as Jesus heard the word that was spoken, he saith unto the ruler of the synagogue, Be not afraid, only believe.
Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live:
corruption_summary: The raisings in the Gospels are recast as resuscitations of the merely comatose, on the strength of the Lord's words that the damsel was not dead but sleepeth; the crowd that laughed him to scorn knew a corpse when they saw one, and he used the same word of Lazarus, who had been four days buried.
corruption_paragraphs: The argument that Jairus' daughter was only in a coma rests on a single clause — the damsel is not dead, but sleepeth — and ignores both the reaction and the usage. Mark records that they laughed him to scorn, which is what professional mourners do when a man contradicts a death they have been hired to lament. And the Lord uses the same figure of Lazarus, telling the disciples plainly, our friend Lazarus sleepeth, and then, when they misunderstood, saying so without the figure: Lazarus is dead. Sleep is the New Testament's regular word for the death of those who will be raised, which is exactly the claim being made in that room.

What the passage is finally about is the authority in the hand and the voice. Christ takes a corpse by the hand, which would defile any other Jew, and speaks two ordinary domestic words in the child's own dialect — not an incantation, not a struggle, but the tone a mother uses in the morning. He did the same at Nain and at Bethany, and he said to Martha what governs every graveside since: I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live. The raisings were signs; the resurrection is the substance, and he is it.
roots_summary: Aramaic talitha (G5008), a maiden or little girl; koumi (G2891), arise, the feminine imperative; Greek anistemi (G450), to rise up.
roots_lines: Aramaic koumi (G2891) — arise; the feminine imperative of qum, to stand up.
Aramaic talitha (G5008) — a young girl, a maiden; Mark preserves the Lord's own syllables.
Greek anistemi (G450) — to rise up, to stand up; straightway the damsel arose.
Greek katagelao (G2606) — to laugh down, to deride; they laughed him to scorn.
Greek ekstasis (G1611) — amazement, astonishment; astonished with a great astonishment.
usage: “Talitha cumi” — the single occurrence, and the Lord's own words kept in his own tongue.
“Be not afraid, only believe” — what he said to the father on the news of the death.
“I am the resurrection, and the life” — the claim the raisings pointed to.
